title: Raindrop Racing — Stokes drag, surface tension, coalescence phase transition
description: Why raindrops merge and accelerate down a window. Stokes drag, surface tension, and a phase transition above a critical radius.

hero.subtitle: Stokes drag · Surface tension · Coalescence phase transition
hero.bio: Watch a raindrop on a window. It sits. It grows slowly. Then suddenly it streaks down, eating other drops as it goes. Two regimes, one threshold. Below a critical radius, the drop is pinned by surface tension. Above it, gravity wins and the drop runs.

manifesto.title: Why do raindrops merge and run?

paragraphs.text: It's raining. You're at a window. A raindrop lands and sits there, slowly growing as smaller drops merge with it. Then, abruptly, it accelerates downward, swallowing every drop in its path. What just happened?

Two forces compete. Gravity pulls the drop down: F_g = ρVg. Surface tension pins it to the glass: F_σ = 2πrσ cos θ, where σ is the surface tension coefficient and θ is the contact angle. The drop stays put while F_σ > F_g — that is, while its radius is below a critical value r* derived by balancing the two.
The critical radius is 1.5 mm. Below it, the drop is a sphere. Above it, the drop is a river.

Once a drop exceeds r*, gravity dominates and the drop accelerates. As it moves, it absorbs smaller drops in its path — each absorption increases its mass, which increases its gravitational force, which accelerates it further. This is the coalescence cascade: a runaway process that converts a quiet field of pinned drops into a single fast streak.

items.title: Force Balance
items.desc: Two forces: F_g = (4/3)πr³ ρg (gravity) vs F_σ = 2πrσ cos θ (surface tension pinning). Critical radius r* = (3σ cos θ / ρg)^(1/2). For water on glass: r* ≈ 1.5 mm.

items.title: Stokes Drag
items.desc: Terminal velocity: once unpinned, the drop reaches terminal velocity v_t = (2/9) (r² ρ g) / η, where η is the dynamic viscosity of air (1.8e-5 Pa·s). A 2 mm drop hits 1 m/s in under 0.1 s.

items.title: Coalescence Cascade
items.desc: Validation: a population of 200 drops with random initial radii is simulated. Drops above r* begin moving. Each absorbed drop increases the parent's radius. Cascade duration to first giant streak: ~6 seconds in simulation time.

items.title: Honest Limitations
items.desc: What this model ignores: wind (the window is not vertical in the model — it is, but no shear), drop deformation during motion (spheres only), evaporation, surface roughness, contact-angle hysteresis. Real glass is dirtier than the model.

paragraphs.text: Every Over Engineer project follows the same six-step pipeline: observe, model, simulate, optimize, visualize, document. Raindrop Racing was observed on the kitchen window during a November storm. The model is force balance plus Stokes drag. The simulation is an event-driven particle system with coalescence detection.

The optimization step here is unusual: there's nothing to optimize. The model has no free parameters that admit optimization — surface tension and viscosity are physical constants. The "optimization" is the choice of numerical scheme. Event-driven integration (step on each collision) beats fixed-step RK4 by a factor of 40 in wall time.

Visualization is the project's deliverable: a 60-second animation showing 200 drops with random initial radii, with one drop seeded above r* at t=0. The cascade begins immediately, and by t=6s a single giant streak dominates the field. The first time you watch it, it looks like real rain on a window. That's the test.
